processing: Black tea dust is cleaned of grit, sieved and winnowed, measured into face and inner layers, steamed and pressed into a brick, then slowly dried at low temperature.
harvest_season: Not a seasonal picking: the brick is made from black tea fragments, so the harvest of the leaf behind it is rarely stated.
appearance_dry: A hard rectangular brick of very fine, dark, glossy tea dust.
appearance_wet: Fine dark particles rather than leaves, which settle as sediment.
taste_profile: Mellow and full with a plain, even aroma; more a strong, sturdy everyday brew than a nuanced one.

brewing.notes: Shave a piece from the brick with a knife and simmer it in a pot, the way brick teas usually are; it takes milk well. A strainer helps because the tea is so fine.

vintage_note: Sold by the brick, usually marked with its factory and production date rather than as a seasonal tea. It keeps for years if dry, as compressed black teas do, but age is not its main selling point.
description:
Despite the name, there is no rice here. Mi Zhuan is a brick pressed entirely from black tea dust, the 'rice' pointing to how fine the particles are. It comes from the Chibi area of southern Hubei, around Zhaoliqiao and Yangloudong, and is the black tea sibling of the region's better-known qing zhuan dark brick.

Making one is more engineering than leaf craft. The dust is cleaned and sorted, divided into a finer face and a coarser inner, then steamed and pressed under heavy force and dried slowly at low heat. The fine particles lock together into a very hard, smooth block.

The cup is deep red, mellow and full, without the leafy high notes of loose black tea. This is a tea to simmer rather than to fuss over in a gaiwan: shave some off, boil it briefly, and add milk if you like. Brick teas of this kind have long been drunk that way in northern and western China.

When buying, look for a clean, undamaged brick with crisp moulded edges from a named factory. Many are bought as display pieces, but they are still perfectly drinkable.
history:
The region's brick tea trade is usually traced to the Qianlong era of the Qing dynasty, when Shanxi merchants set up tea works at Yangloudong and reshaped earlier 'maohe' tea into square bricks, producing both qing zhuan and mi zhuan.

The Zhaoliqiao factory, the name most closely tied to this tea today, moved from Yangloudong to Zhaoliqiao in 1953. The local brick tea technique is on China's national intangible heritage list, and Chibi promotes itself as the home of rice brick tea.
